question: Hysterosalpingogram (HSG) primarily uses which type of radiation imaging?
explanation:
• HSG is an X-ray fluoroscopic study with contrast to assess tubal patency.
• Memory-based NORCET theme.
citation: D.C. Dutta's Textbook of Gynecology, 8e

question: Whole blood stored in blood bank is typically kept at approximately:
explanation:
• RBC storage: 2–6°C is standard cold chain.
• Frequently asked in competitive nursing exams.
citation: NACO / National Blood Transfusion Council, Standards for Blood Banks & Blood Transfusion Services (2007)

question: Thanatology is the study of:
explanation:
• Thanatology relates to death, dying, and bereavement.
• NORCET memory-based recall question.
citation: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 9e

question: Honey should be introduced in infant weaning typically:
explanation:
• Honey is avoided <12 months due to infant botulism risk.
• Aligns with common PYQ discussions.
citation: CDC, Botulism: Prevention (infant botulism guidance, 2021)

question: A marker associated with neural tube defects in amniotic fluid includes:
explanation:
• Elevated AFP and AChE patterns support NTD screening context.
• Simplified for MCQ practice.
citation: D.C. Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics, 9e

question: Sarcopenia refers to:
options: B. Age-related loss of muscle mass and strength
explanation:
• Sarcopenia = muscle loss with aging.
• NORCET general science theme.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e

question: Synthetic form of vitamin K often referenced in exams:
explanation:
• Menadione is synthetic vitamin K3; phylloquinone is K1 natural.
• Verify with standard texts.
citation: K.D. Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8e

question: Direct Coombs test detects:
options: B. Antibody attached to RBC surface
explanation:
• Direct antiglobulin test detects antibodies on RBCs.
• High-yield hematology.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e

question: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) typically occurs after intubation for at least:
explanation:
• VAP definitions often use ventilation >48–72 hours.
• Guidelines vary slightly; this is exam-oriented.
citation: IDSA/ATS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Hospital-Acquired and Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (2016)

question: Log roll technique for spinal precautions typically needs at least:
explanation:
• Log roll for spinal injury: usually 3–4 staff to maintain alignment.
• Some sources cite minimum 3; option reflects coordinated team roll.
citation: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 9e

question: T lymphocytes mature primarily in:
explanation:
• T cells mature in thymus; B cells in bone marrow.
• Very high yield.
citation: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14e

question: BLS sequence for unresponsive adult without pulse:
explanation: • AHA BLS: start chest compressions first (C-A-B) for adults.
citation: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care (2020)

question: Parkland formula for fluid resuscitation in burns uses:
options: C. 4 mL × kg × %TBSA lactated Ringer’s in 24h
explanation:
• Parkland: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA LR (half in 8h, half in 16h).
• Classic NORCET style.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e

question: PM-JAY provides health coverage up to (approx) per family per year:
explanation:
• Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY coverage commonly cited as ₹5 lakh/family/year.
• Verify official updates.
citation: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 26e

question: MTP Act (as commonly tested) allows termination up to:
options: C. 24 weeks in many specified situations
explanation:
• Indian MTP amendments extended gestational limits in defined categories; exams often cite up to 24 weeks context.
• Cross-check latest statute for your exam cycle.
citation: Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 (India)

question: Spinal anesthesia monitoring should especially watch for:
explanation:
• Sympathetic block → hypotension/bradycardia common.
• NORCET clinical theme.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e

question: Hand rub with alcohol-based sanitizer effective duration commonly taught:
explanation:
• WHO: rub until dry, ~20–30 seconds.
• Fundamentals high yield.
citation: WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care (2009)

question: Yellow bio-medical waste bag is used for:
options: B. Infectious/pathological/certain contaminated wastes per BMW rules
explanation:
• BMW rule categories: yellow bag for specified infectious/soiled wastes (contextual).
• Follow latest national guidelines.
citation: Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 (Government of India, as amended)

question: Exclusive breastfeeding recommended for:
explanation:
• WHO: exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months.
• Standard CHN question.
citation: WHO Global Strategy for Infant and Young Child Feeding (2003)

question: Pulse polio immunization is an example of:
explanation:
• Oral polio vaccine campaigns provide active immunity.
• CHN program classic.
citation: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 26e

question: Early sign of hypovolemic shock may include:
explanation: In compensated hypovolemic shock the baroreceptors sense the falling stroke volume and trigger a sympathetic surge, so the heart rate climbs before the blood pressure falls — tachycardia with a weak, thready pulse is the earliest reliable sign. Blood pressure is held up by vasoconstriction until roughly 30% of the circulating volume is lost, so hypertension is not expected and a normal reading can be falsely reassuring. That same vasoconstriction makes the skin cool, pale and clammy rather than warm and flushed (warm flushed skin belongs to early distributive/septic shock), and the reduced stroke volume gives a thready, not a bounding, pulse.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e

question: Sterile field is considered contaminated if:
options: B. Sterile gloved hand drops below waist level
explanation: A sterile field is sterile only above waist/table level and within the nurse's line of vision, so a sterile gloved hand that drops below the waist can no longer be observed and is considered contaminated. Sterility is likewise lost by strike-through — moisture soaking through a drape from an unsterile surface — or by turning away from or leaving the field unattended. Transferring items with sterile forceps is correct technique and quiet talking over a masked field is permitted, so neither of those breaks asepsis.
citation: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 9e

question: Antidote for opioid overdose:
explanation: Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist with high affinity for the μ receptor; given IV/IM/intranasally it displaces the opioid within 1–2 minutes and reverses the respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils and coma of overdose. Its half-life is shorter than that of most opioids, so re-sedation can occur and repeat boluses or an infusion may be required. Flumazenil is the benzodiazepine antagonist, atropine treats organophosphate/muscarinic poisoning, and vitamin K reverses warfarin — none of them acts at the opioid receptor.
citation: K.D. Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8e

question: Normal fetal heart rate baseline typically:
explanation: The normal baseline fetal heart rate is 110–160 bpm, read over a 10-minute window after excluding accelerations, decelerations and periods of marked variability. A sustained rate below 110 bpm is bradycardia — suggesting hypoxia, cord compression or congenital heart block — which rules out the 80–100 and 60–90 bpm options. A rate above 160 bpm is tachycardia, seen with maternal fever, chorioamnionitis, drugs or early fetal compromise, so 170–190 bpm is also abnormal.
citation: D.C. Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics, 9e

question: ASHA worker is primarily:
options: B. Community health volunteer under NRHM
explanation: The Accredited Social Health Activist is a female village-resident volunteer (usually 25–45 years, preferably schooled to class 8) selected under the National Rural Health Mission from 2005, at about one ASHA per 1000 rural population. She is honorary and paid by performance-linked incentives rather than a salary, and works as the bridge between the community and the health system — mobilising for immunisation, antenatal care and institutional delivery, escorting patients, and providing DOTS and simple first-contact remedies from her drug kit. She is not a doctor, laboratory technician or pharmacist; those are facility-based cadres posted at the sub-centre, PHC and above.
citation: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 26e

question: Therapeutic communication includes:
explanation: Therapeutic communication is goal-directed and patient-centred, and active listening — attending, using purposeful silence, reflecting and clarifying — is its core technique because it conveys acceptance and invites the patient to express feelings. False reassurance such as 'everything will be fine' dismisses a real concern and stops further disclosure, while abruptly changing the topic signals the nurse's own discomfort and closes off what the patient needed to explore. Criticising or judging the patient destroys trust; all three are classic non-therapeutic blocking responses.
citation: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 9e

question: Weight doubles by approximately:
explanation: A term newborn loses up to 10% of birth weight in the first week, regains it by about day 10, and then gains roughly 25–30 g/day, so birth weight doubles by about 5 months. The same growth rule continues with tripling by 1 year and quadrupling by 2 years, which is why the 12-month and 2-year options describe later milestones. At 3 months the infant has usually added only about half its birth weight again, so doubling has not yet happened.
citation: Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 9e

question: Liver is located mainly in:
explanation: The liver occupies mainly the right hypochondrium and epigastrium — clinically the right upper quadrant — lying under the right dome of the diaphragm and sheltered by ribs 7–11, with only the smaller left lobe crossing into the left hypochondrium. This is why liver span is percussed in the right midclavicular line and why right-upper-quadrant pain and tenderness point to hepatobiliary disease. The liver is intraperitoneal apart from its small bare area, so it is not a retroperitoneal organ, and it never lies in the pelvis.
citation: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4e

question: Article 21 of Indian Constitution relates to:
options: B. Protection of life and personal liberty
explanation: Article 21 provides that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law, and the Supreme Court has read into it the right to health, emergency medical treatment, privacy and a life with dignity — the constitutional footing usually cited in nursing ethics and jurisprudence. Free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 is a separate provision, Article 21A, and freedom of speech and expression falls under Article 19(1)(a). The right to property ceased to be a fundamental right after the 44th Amendment and now survives as a constitutional right under Article 300A.
citation: The Constitution of India, Article 21

question: Acid-fast bacillus seen in:
explanation: Acid-fastness comes from the mycolic-acid-rich waxy cell wall of mycobacteria, which holds carbol fuchsin even after decolourisation with acid-alcohol; on Ziehl-Neelsen staining Mycobacterium tuberculosis appears as slender red beaded bacilli against a blue counterstained background. Staphylococcus and E. coli lack mycolic acids and decolourise readily, so they are demonstrated as a gram-positive coccus and a gram-negative bacillus respectively. Candida is a fungus, shown by KOH mount, Gram stain or culture, not by acid-fast staining.
citation: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 11e

question: The earliest electrocardiographic change expected in a patient whose serum potassium is rising is:
explanation: Hyperkalaemia raises the resting membrane potential and accelerates repolarisation, so the first ECG sign — usually at a serum potassium of about 5.5–6.5 mEq/L — is a tall, narrow, peaked T wave, followed later by a flattened P wave, a prolonged PR interval and a widened QRS. Sine-wave complexes are the most tempting distractor because they do occur in hyperkalaemia, but only as a pre-terminal change at very high levels immediately before ventricular fibrillation or asystole. Prominent U waves with T-wave flattening indicate hypokalaemia, and a prolonged QT interval is the classical change of hypocalcaemia.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e — Fluid and Electrolyte Balance

question: Which method is the gold standard for confirming the position of a newly inserted nasogastric tube before the first feed?
options: A. Auscultating over the epigastrium while injecting air
B. Testing the aspirate with pH indicator paper
C. Radiographic visualisation of the tube tip
D. Observing for bubbling when the tube end is held in water
explanation: An X-ray that shows the radio-opaque tip below the diaphragm and within the stomach is the only method that reliably excludes respiratory or oesophageal placement, so it is the definitive check before the first feed or medication. Testing an aspirate with pH paper is the most tempting alternative and is the accepted first-line bedside check when a value of 5.5 or less is obtained, but it fails when no aspirate can be withdrawn or the patient is on acid-suppressing drugs. The 'whoosh test' of auscultating injected air has been abandoned as unsafe, because air pushed through a tube misplaced in the bronchus or oesophagus can still be heard over the epigastrium, and bubbling in water is neither sensitive nor specific.
citation: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 9e — Nutrition

question: Before giving a scheduled oral dose of digoxin to an adult, the nurse counts the apical pulse for one full minute. The dose should be withheld and the physician informed if the rate is below:
explanation: Digoxin increases vagal tone and slows conduction through the AV node, so bradycardia is an early marker of excessive effect; the standard nursing rule is to withhold the dose and report an adult apical rate below 60 beats/min, the corresponding cut-offs being about 70/min in a child and 90–110/min in an infant. Rates of 80–100/min are normal or even fast and give no reason to omit a prescribed dose, so those options would deny the patient treatment. The nurse should also check serum potassium, because hypokalaemia from concurrent loop diuretics sensitises the myocardium and can produce toxicity even at therapeutic digoxin levels.
citation: K.D. Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8e — Drugs for Heart Failure

question: In the active management of the third stage of labour, the uterotonic recommended as the first choice for all women immediately after birth of the baby is:
explanation: Oxytocin 10 IU given intramuscularly within one minute of birth is the uterotonic of choice for every delivery because it acts within two to three minutes, is effective in preventing postpartum haemorrhage and has few side effects. Methylergometrine is the most tempting alternative, and it is a legitimate second choice where oxytocin is unavailable, but it is contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia and heart disease and causes marked nausea and vomiting. Misoprostol 600 µg is reserved for settings without a skilled birth attendant or a cold chain, and carboprost is a treatment for established atonic haemorrhage rather than routine prophylaxis.
citation: WHO Recommendations for the Prevention and Treatment of Postpartum Haemorrhage

question: Which vaccine of the Universal Immunization Programme is the most heat-sensitive and is therefore kept in the deep freezer at district level?
explanation: Oral polio vaccine is the most heat-labile vaccine in the programme, which is why it is stored at −15 to −25 °C in the deep freezer at regional and district stores and is placed closest to the ice packs in the vaccine carrier during outreach sessions. BCG is the tempting choice because it is also heat- and light-sensitive, but it is kept in the ice-lined refrigerator at +2 to +8 °C, not frozen at the peripheral level. DPT and hepatitis B are damaged by freezing rather than by heat, so they must never be put in the deep freezer or allowed to touch conditioned ice packs directly.
citation: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 26e — Immunity and Immunization

question: The accepted therapeutic serum lithium concentration during maintenance treatment of bipolar disorder is:
explanation: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, and maintenance levels are kept at 0.6–1.2 mEq/L measured on a sample drawn 12 hours after the last dose. A level of 1.5–2.0 mEq/L is the most tempting distractor because it looks like a plausible upper range, but it is already toxic, producing coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, slurred speech and ataxia, and above 2.5 mEq/L seizures, renal failure and death can follow. Levels below about 0.6 mEq/L are subtherapeutic for relapse prevention, and the patient must be taught to keep salt and fluid intake steady, since dehydration, a low-sodium diet, thiazides and NSAIDs all push the level up.
citation: K.D. Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8e — Drugs Used in Mental Illness

question: BCG vaccine is administered to an infant by which route and at which site?
options: A. Intradermally over the left upper arm at the insertion of the deltoid
B. Subcutaneously over the right upper arm
C. Intramuscularly into the anterolateral aspect of the thigh
explanation: BCG is given strictly intradermally with a tuberculin syringe into the skin over the insertion of the left deltoid, 0.05 mL for an infant under one month and 0.1 mL thereafter, and a correct injection raises a blanched wheal of about 5 mm. The subcutaneous option is the tempting one because measles-rubella vaccine is given subcutaneously in the upper arm, but depositing BCG below the dermis causes a cold abscess and regional lymphadenitis instead of the intended papule, ulcer and scar. The anterolateral thigh is the intramuscular site for pentavalent vaccine, and the oral route belongs to polio and rotavirus vaccines.
citation: Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 9e — Immunization

question: In an adult the spinal cord normally terminates as the conus medullaris at the level of:
explanation: In the adult the cord tapers into the conus medullaris at the lower border of L1, opposite the L1–L2 disc, and continues below only as the filum terminale among the nerve roots of the cauda equina. The L3 option is tempting because the cord does reach L3 in the newborn, which is why a lower interspace is chosen in infants, but it ascends relatively as the vertebral column grows faster than the cord. This anatomy is why lumbar puncture and spinal anaesthesia are performed at L3–L4 or L4–L5, along the line joining the highest points of the iliac crests, where only mobile cauda equina roots lie in the path of the needle.
citation: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4e — Back

question: The National Health Policy 2017 set a target of raising public health expenditure to what proportion of the gross domestic product?
explanation: The National Health Policy 2017 commits the government to increasing public health expenditure in a time-bound manner to 2.5% of GDP by 2025, together with targets such as raising life expectancy to 70 years and cutting under-five mortality to 23 per 1000 live births. Options of 1.5% and 2% are tempting because public spending stood at roughly 1.15% of GDP when the policy was framed, so they describe the starting position rather than the goal. Around 5% of GDP is what many high-income countries spend and what advocacy groups urge, but no such figure appears in the policy.
citation: National Health Policy 2017, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

question: The standard cycle for sterilising surgical dressings in an autoclave is:
options: A. 121 °C at 15 lb per square inch for 15 minutes
B. 100 °C at atmospheric pressure for 30 minutes
explanation: Saturated steam under pressure kills spores by coagulating microbial proteins, and the standard autoclave cycle is a holding time of 15 minutes at 121 °C and 15 lb per square inch, checked with a Geobacillus stearothermophilus spore strip, Browne's tube or autoclave tape. The 160 °C for 2 hours option is the most tempting because it also sterilises, but that is the hot-air oven cycle for dry heat, used for glassware, powders, oils and sharp instruments that steam would blunt or corrode. Boiling at 100 °C only disinfects since spores survive it, and 63 °C for 30 minutes is the holder method of pasteurisation, which does not sterilise at all.
citation: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 11e — Sterilization and Disinfection

question: Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber of a closed chest drainage system throughout inspiration and expiration indicates:
options: A. The lung has fully re-expanded
B. An air leak in the patient or the drainage system
C. Correct functioning of the suction control chamber
D. That the drainage tubing is kinked or obstructed
explanation: The water seal works as a one-way valve, so bubbling there means air is still leaving the pleural space; intermittent bubbling on expiration or coughing is expected while a pneumothorax resolves, but bubbling through the entire respiratory cycle signals a leak, which the nurse localises by briefly clamping along the tubing from the chest downwards and by inspecting the insertion-site dressing. Mistaking it for normal suction is the commonest error — gentle continuous bubbling is expected in the suction-control chamber, never in the water seal. Full re-expansion produces the opposite picture, with bubbling stopped and tidalling of the fluid column absent, and an obstructed tube also abolishes tidalling but with worsening respiratory distress.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e — Management of Patients with Chest and Lower Respiratory Tract Disorders

question: A bed-bound patient has intact skin over the sacrum with localised redness that does not blanch on finger pressure. This pressure injury is staged as:
explanation: Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin is the definition of a stage 1 pressure injury, and it is distinguished at the bedside from ordinary reactive hyperaemia, which blanches white under a finger and returns to pink when the pressure is released. Stage 2 is the most tempting answer, but it requires partial-thickness loss of dermis presenting as a shallow open ulcer or an intact or ruptured serum-filled blister, and this patient's skin is unbroken. Stage 3 involves full-thickness loss with visible subcutaneous fat, and an injury is called unstageable only when slough or eschar conceals the depth of the wound bed.
citation: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 9e — Skin Integrity and Wound Care

question: A patient on first-line antitubercular treatment reports blurred vision and difficulty distinguishing red from green. The drug most likely responsible is:
explanation: Ethambutol causes a dose-dependent retrobulbar (optic) neuritis with reduced visual acuity and loss of red-green colour discrimination, so visual acuity and colour vision are checked at baseline and periodically, and the drug is stopped at the first symptom, after which recovery is usual. Isoniazid is the most tempting alternative because it is also neurotoxic, but its characteristic lesion is a peripheral sensory neuropathy from pyridoxine antagonism, prevented by pyridoxine 10 mg daily. Rifampicin colours urine, tears and sweat orange-red and may cause hepatitis, and pyrazinamide typically raises serum uric acid and causes arthralgia.
citation: K.D. Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8e — Antitubercular Drugs

question: On the cervicograph of the partograph, the alert line represents cervical dilatation progressing at a rate of:
explanation: The alert line runs from the start of the active phase to full dilatation at a slope of 1 cm per hour, and plotting to the right of it warns that labour is slower than expected — in a peripheral unit that is the signal to transfer the woman to a centre with operative facilities. The action line is drawn parallel to it and four hours to its right, and crossing that line calls for assessment and intervention such as amniotomy or oxytocin augmentation. A rate of 0.5 cm per hour is frank protraction rather than the reference slope, and 1.5–2 cm per hour describes faster-than-average progress.
citation: D.C. Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics, 9e — Normal Labour

question: The reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration solution recommended for the management of diarrhoea has a total osmolarity of:
explanation: The low-osmolarity formula contains sodium 75, glucose 75, chloride 65, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L, giving a total osmolarity of 245 mOsm/L, and the lower osmotic load shortens the episode, reduces stool output and cuts the need for unscheduled intravenous fluid. The 311 mOsm/L option is the most tempting because that was the original WHO formula taught for two decades before it was replaced in 2002, and it carried a higher risk of hypernatraemia. The remaining values do not correspond to any recommended formulation.
citation: WHO/UNICEF Joint Statement: Clinical Management of Acute Diarrhoea

question: Three days after starting haloperidol a patient develops a temperature of 40 °C, lead-pipe muscle rigidity, fluctuating consciousness, labile blood pressure and a markedly raised creatine kinase. The nurse should suspect:
explanation: Hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, altered sensorium and autonomic instability with a raised creatine kinase and leucocytosis after a dopamine-blocking drug constitute neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a medical emergency managed by stopping the antipsychotic, aggressive cooling and hydration, and dantrolene or bromocriptine in severe cases. Serotonin syndrome is the closest mimic and the most tempting distractor, but it follows serotonergic drugs such as SSRIs and is marked by hyperreflexia, inducible clonus, dilated pupils and diarrhoea rather than rigid, hyporeflexic limbs. An acute dystonic reaction produces torticollis, oculogyric crisis or trismus without fever, and tardive dyskinesia is a late choreiform movement disorder appearing after months to years of treatment.
citation: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12e — Medication-Induced Movement Disorders

question: The anterior fontanelle of a normally developing infant closes by:
explanation: The diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle at the junction of the coronal and sagittal sutures normally closes between 12 and 18 months, and until then it is a clinical window that is depressed in dehydration and tense or bulging when intracranial pressure rises. The 6–8 week option is the tempting one because that is when the small triangular posterior fontanelle closes. Closure well before a year suggests craniosynostosis or microcephaly, while persistence beyond 18 months is seen in rickets, hypothyroidism, hydrocephalus and Down syndrome.
citation: Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 9e — Normal Growth and Its Disorders

question: In a healthy adult the apex beat is normally palpated in the:
options: A. Second intercostal space at the right sternal border
B. Fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border
C. Fifth left intercostal space in the midclavicular line
D. Fifth left intercostal space in the anterior axillary line
explanation: The apex beat is the lowest and most lateral point at which the cardiac impulse is felt, normally in the fifth left intercostal space just medial to or in the midclavicular line, roughly 9 cm from the midline, and it corresponds to the mitral auscultatory area. Displacement to the anterior axillary line is the most tempting option because the interspace is the same, but it is abnormal and indicates cardiomegaly from left ventricular dilatation or a mediastinal shift caused by pleural effusion, pneumothorax or collapse. The second right intercostal space is the aortic area and the fourth left parasternal space the tricuspid area — auscultation landmarks rather than the site of the apex beat.
citation: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4e — Thorax

question: International Nurses Day is observed every year on 12 May because that date marks the:
options: A. Founding of the International Council of Nurses
B. Constitution of the Indian Nursing Council
C. Anniversary of the first World Health Assembly
D. Birth anniversary of Florence Nightingale
explanation: The International Council of Nurses has marked 12 May, the birth anniversary of Florence Nightingale, as International Nurses Day since 1965 and issues an annual theme and resource kit for the profession. The founding of the ICN is the most tempting distractor, but the council was established in 1899 in London and that event has its own separate history. The Indian Nursing Council was constituted under the Indian Nursing Council Act of 1947 and the first World Health Assembly met in June 1948, so neither is commemorated on this date.
citation: International Council of Nurses — International Nurses Day

question: The organism most commonly responsible for catheter-associated urinary tract infection is:
explanation: Escherichia coli, a gram-negative enteric bacillus from the patient's own faecal flora, ascends the periurethral space and the biofilm on the catheter surface and remains the single commonest isolate in catheter-associated urinary tract infection — which is why perineal hygiene, a closed drainage system, keeping the bag below bladder level and removing the catheter at the earliest opportunity are the core preventive measures. Candida is the most tempting alternative because it is recovered increasingly often after prolonged catheterisation, in diabetics and after broad-spectrum antibiotics, but it is still far less frequent overall. Staphylococcus aureus is chiefly a wound and bloodstream pathogen, and Clostridioides difficile causes antibiotic-associated colitis, not urinary infection.
citation: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 11e — Hospital-Acquired Infections

question: Which cardiac biomarker is the most specific for myocardial injury and remains elevated for up to 10–14 days after an infarction?
options: D. Cardiac troponin I or T
explanation: Cardiac troponins I and T are structural proteins of the cardiac contractile apparatus, so they are highly specific for myocardial injury; they begin to rise in 3–4 hours, peak at about 24 hours and stay detectable for 10–14 days, which is what allows an infarct to be diagnosed in a patient who presents several days late. Creatine kinase-MB is the most tempting distractor, but it returns to normal within 48–72 hours, so its value now lies in detecting re-infarction rather than late diagnosis. Myoglobin rises earliest, within 1–3 hours, but is released from skeletal muscle as well and is therefore non-specific, and aspartate aminotransferase is an obsolete marker raised in liver and muscle disease alike.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e — Management of Patients with Coronary Vascular Disorders

question: Oxygen delivered by nasal cannula at 4 litres per minute provides an approximate inspired oxygen concentration of:
explanation: A nasal cannula is a low-flow device in which each additional litre per minute adds roughly 4% to the 21% oxygen of room air, so 1 L/min gives about 24% and 4 L/min about 36%, although the delivered concentration varies with the patient's tidal volume and respiratory rate. The 28% option is the commonest trap because it corresponds to 2 L/min, one step short of the flow in the question. Flows above 6 L/min add little and dry and ulcerate the nasal mucosa, and a concentration near 60% needs a partial rebreathing or non-rebreathing mask with a reservoir bag.
citation: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 9e — Oxygenation

question: Which laboratory test is used to monitor a patient receiving a continuous intravenous infusion of unfractionated heparin?
explanation: Unfractionated heparin activates antithrombin and thereby inhibits thrombin and factor Xa, prolonging the intrinsic pathway, so the infusion is titrated against an activated partial thromboplastin time kept at about 1.5–2.5 times the control value. Prothrombin time with INR is the most tempting answer, but it monitors warfarin, which depletes the vitamin K-dependent factors of the extrinsic pathway; the two tests are used together only while a patient is being bridged from heparin to warfarin. Bleeding time reflects platelet-vessel interaction and is not used for titrating anticoagulants, though the platelet count is followed separately to detect heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and the ESR is a non-specific inflammatory marker.
citation: K.D. Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8e — Drugs Affecting Coagulation, Bleeding and Thrombosis

question: A woman with eclampsia is receiving magnesium sulphate. The earliest clinical sign of magnesium toxicity the nurse must watch for is:
options: A. Loss of the patellar (knee-jerk) reflex
B. Respiratory rate below 12 per minute
C. Urine output below 30 mL per hour
explanation: Deep tendon reflexes disappear at a serum magnesium of roughly 8–10 mEq/L, well before respiratory depression at about 12 mEq/L and cardiac arrest above 25 mEq/L, so an absent knee jerk is the earliest warning and the maintenance dose is withheld the moment it is lost. A respiratory rate under 12–16 per minute is the most tempting answer because it is also monitored before every dose, but it is a later and far more dangerous sign, by which stage calcium gluconate 1 g intravenously must be given as the antidote. Urine output below 30 mL per hour is checked because magnesium is excreted by the kidney and oliguria causes accumulation, but that is a risk factor for toxicity rather than a sign of it.
citation: D.C. Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics, 9e — Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy

question: As per national norms, one sub-centre (health and wellness centre) in a plain area is established for a population of:
explanation: A sub-centre serves 5,000 people in plain areas and is the most peripheral contact point between the community and the health system, staffed by a female health worker (ANM) and a male health worker under the supervision of the health assistant. The 3,000 option is the most tempting because that is the same norm applied to hilly, tribal and desert areas, where terrain limits access. A primary health centre covers 30,000 in the plains and 20,000 in hilly or tribal areas, and a community health centre covers 1,20,000 and 80,000 respectively.
citation: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 26e — Health Care of the Community
